name: Blue light acne device
lead: A blue light acne device is a handheld wand, mask or panel that emits visible blue light, typically in the 405 to 470 nanometre range, onto acne-prone skin for several minutes per session. Clinics use higher-powered units, while consumer devices are lower in power.

Blue light is used as a drug-free option for mild to moderate inflammatory acne. Its proposed mechanism is that Cutibacterium acnes produces porphyrins that absorb blue light and generate reactive oxygen species that damage the bacterium, and that the light may also have mild anti-inflammatory effects.

A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Annals of Family Medicine, a 2021 systematic review, and a Cochrane-based review of light therapies for acne have examined the trials.[1][2][3] Reviewers describe the studies as generally small, short and at risk of bias, so effectiveness relative to standard treatments is uncertain. Home devices are weaker than clinic units.

paras: Devices come as wands that are held over blemishes, masks, and panels, sometimes combining blue with red light. Blue light therapy sits within the wider field of phototherapy, which also includes bright-light therapy for mood, ultraviolet phototherapy for psoriasis and eczema, and photodynamic therapy.[4]

The bacterium Cutibacterium acnes (formerly Propionibacterium acnes) makes porphyrins, which absorb light around the blue range. Excited porphyrins are proposed to produce reactive oxygen species that kill or damage the bacteria. Blue light is also suggested to have a mild anti-inflammatory action on the skin. Grokipedia describes acne treatment via blue-red combinations as killing P. acnes.[4]

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses report that blue light can reduce acne lesion counts, but the included trials are small, short and at risk of bias, so its performance against standard treatments remains unclear.[1][2] The Cochrane-derived review of light therapies for acne graded the evidence with GRADE.[3] Combined blue and red light may perform better than blue alone in the short term. A review of home-based dermatology devices graded LED acne treatment as supported by three randomized trials, citing one trial with 77% and 54% reductions in inflammatory and non-inflammatory lesions, and noted there were no double-blinded RCTs among home devices overall and little long-term data.[5]

Reported side effects are minor, including temporary dryness, redness or, in one case reported in a home-device review, erythema and desquamation.[5] Eye protection is generally advised, and photosensitivity disorders or photosensitising medicines are contraindications for light therapy in general.[4]

Human trials have been pooled in several reviews. A 2019 systematic review and meta-analysis of blue-light therapy for acne vulgaris,[1] a 2021 systematic review of the effect of blue light on acne,[2] and the abridged Cochrane review of light therapies for acne with GRADE assessments[3] all assess clinical trials; they describe small, short studies with risk of bias. A review of home-based dermatology devices included three randomized trials of LED acne treatment.[5]
